items.prompt: After a successful login, where does the actual session data (e.g. which user this is) get stored?
choices: Inside the cookie itself, fully encoded as readable text
In a server-side record, referenced by an ID the cookie carries
In the URL of every single request the browser ever sends
Nowhere — the browser simply re-sends the password each time
items.explanation: A traditional session cookie carries only an opaque ID. The actual data — which user, what permissions — is stored server-side, indexed by that ID. The cookie is a pointer, not the payload.
items.reflection: The session-ID-as-pointer trick isn't special to web auth — it's the same shape as a coat-check ticket, a library hold slip, or a short URL: a small, meaningless-looking token that only works because something else, somewhere, maps it back to the real thing. The question worth asking about any such system: what happens to the token's holder if that 'somewhere else' goes away?

items.prompt: A teammate says 'the cookie contains the user's login info.' For a classic session-based login, is that accurate?
choices: Yes, cookies always contain the entire user record in plain text
No — the cookie usually only carries a session ID; the record lives server-side
No — cookies can never carry any identifying data whatsoever
Yes, but only when the logged-in user happens to be an admin
items.explanation: For session-based auth, the cookie is deliberately kept small and opaque — just an ID. The server looks that ID up in its own store to find the actual user record.
items.reflection: The session-ID-as-pointer trick isn't special to web auth — it's the same shape as a coat-check ticket, a library hold slip, or a short URL: a small, meaningless-looking token that only works because something else, somewhere, maps it back to the real thing. The question worth asking about any such system: what happens to the token's holder if that 'somewhere else' goes away?

items.prompt: A browser extension silently blocks the Set-Cookie response header on login. What happens on the user's very next request?
choices: Nothing — the server remembers the login independently of any cookie
The browser never stored a session ID, so the server has nothing to look up and treats the user as logged out
The server automatically re-sends the username and password for them
The load balancer detects the missing cookie and issues one itself
items.explanation: The session ID only reaches the server again because the browser stored it and resends it automatically. If the cookie never gets stored in the first place, there's no ID to look up on the next request — mechanically identical to never having logged in.
items.reflection: The session-ID-as-pointer trick isn't special to web auth — it's the same shape as a coat-check ticket, a library hold slip, or a short URL: a small, meaningless-looking token that only works because something else, somewhere, maps it back to the real thing. The question worth asking about any such system: what happens to the token's holder if that 'somewhere else' goes away?

items.prompt: What does a session ID let a server do?
choices: Encrypt the user's password
Look up the matching session record
Skip authentication entirely
Route the request to a CDN
items.explanation: A session ID is a lookup key — the server uses it to find the session record it already stored at login.

items.prompt: Which response header does a server use to hand a session ID to the browser after login?
choices: Set-Cookie
Content-Length
Authorization
Location
items.explanation: Set-Cookie is the header a server uses to tell the browser to store a value — in this case, the session ID.

items.prompt: Does application JavaScript need to manually attach a stored cookie to every later request?
choices: Yes, every single request needs explicit code for this
No — the browser attaches matching cookies automatically
Only for POST requests
Only if the server asks nicely in the response body
items.explanation: Cookie resending is a browser behavior that happens automatically for matching requests — no app code has to trigger it.

items.prompt: Is the full user record typically stored inside the session cookie itself?
choices: Yes, always
No — just an opaque ID; the record lives server-side
Only for admin accounts
Only on the first request after login
items.explanation: Classic session cookies are deliberately small and opaque — the actual record stays server-side, indexed by the ID.

items.prompt: What does the server keep, indexed by session ID?
choices: A session record — usually a user ID plus some metadata
A copy of the browser's entire request history
The user's plaintext password
A list of every cookie ever issued by any server
items.explanation: A session record is normally just a user ID plus whatever metadata the app needs — not a password, not a request log.

items.prompt: Which header does the browser use to resend a stored cookie on later requests?
choices: Cookie
Set-Cookie
Referer
Accept
items.explanation: Set-Cookie is how the server sends a cookie to the browser; Cookie is how the browser sends it back on later requests.

items.prompt: If a cookie only carries an opaque session ID, how does the server know who's asking?
choices: It looks the ID up in its own session store
It decodes the ID directly into a user record
It asks the browser to resend the password
It can't — opaque IDs can never be resolved
items.explanation: An opaque ID means the ID itself carries no information — the server has to look it up against where it stored the matching record.

items.prompt: Which of these three fixes removes the need for any server to keep session data at all?
choices: Sticky sessions
A shared session store (e.g. Redis)
A stateless token (JWT)
None of them — some server-side storage is always required
items.explanation: A stateless token carries its own data in the request, so no server anywhere needs to store anything about the session. Sticky sessions and a shared store both still keep the data on a server — one on a single machine, one centralized.

items.prompt: Which fix adds an extra network round trip to every single request, in exchange for working across any number of servers?
choices: Sticky sessions, which pin a user to one server
A shared session store (e.g. Redis)
A stateless token (JWT), carried on the client
All three fixes, equally, in exactly the same way
items.explanation: A shared store fixes the multi-server problem, but every request now needs a lookup against that store — a real, per-request network cost that sticky sessions and JWTs don't have.

items.prompt: A new hire proposes sticky sessions as 'basically the same thing' as a stateless token, since both let a user keep working across multiple servers. What's the flaw in that comparison?
choices: There's no flaw — the two approaches are functionally identical
Sticky sessions still depend on one specific server's memory surviving; a stateless token depends on nothing server-side at all
Stateless tokens are slower because they require a database lookup on every request
Sticky sessions are actually the more modern, more scalable of the two approaches
items.explanation: Sticky sessions only route consistently — they don't remove the underlying fragility of storing the session in one server's RAM. A stateless token removes the server-side dependency entirely; sticky sessions just make it less visible until that one server goes away.

items.prompt: What does 'sticky sessions' mean?
choices: The load balancer always routes a given user to the same server
Every server shares one database
Tokens never expire
Cookies are encrypted before sending
items.explanation: Sticky sessions is a load-balancer configuration: pin a user to a specific backend server.

items.prompt: What's the main downside of sticky sessions?
choices: They break the moment the pinned server restarts or is removed
They require a cryptographic signature on every request
They can only be used with JWTs
They make login slower by design
items.explanation: Sticky sessions keep working only as long as the one pinned server is alive — remove it, and the session is gone.

items.prompt: What's the main cost of a shared session store like Redis?
choices: Every request needs an extra network hop to look the session up
It can only store one session at a time
It requires the client to hold a cryptographic key
It cannot work with cookies at all
items.explanation: A shared store removes the single-server dependency, but every request now pays a network round trip to query it.

items.prompt: What's the main trade-off of a stateless token (JWT) compared to the other two fixes?
choices: It can't easily be 'un-issued' once handed out
It requires every server to share a single database
It only works if the user never changes IP address
It cannot be verified without a network call
items.explanation: A JWT removes the server-side store entirely, but that also means there's no record to delete if you need to revoke it early.

items.prompt: Which fix keeps session data on exactly one specific machine?
choices: Sticky sessions
Shared session store
Stateless tokens
All three, equally
items.explanation: Sticky sessions route to one machine, and that machine's own memory is the only place the session data lives.

items.prompt: Which fix centralizes session data so any server can read it, at the cost of a lookup?
choices: A shared session store (e.g. Redis)
Sticky sessions
A stateless token
None of these approaches centralize anything
items.explanation: A shared store is the 'centralize it' option — every server can reach the same data, but each read/write costs a round trip.

items.prompt: Which fix makes the session data travel inside the request itself?
choices: A stateless token (JWT)
Sticky sessions
A shared session store
None of these
items.explanation: That's the defining trait of a stateless token — the data rides along with the request, so there's nothing to store or look up server-side.

items.prompt: A JWT looks like header.payload.signature. What does the middle part (payload) contain?
choices: The algorithm and key type used to sign the token
The claims — user ID, expiry, and any app-specific data
The cryptographic proof of the token's integrity
Nothing — that segment is reserved for future use
items.explanation: The payload holds the claims: sub (user), exp (expiry), and whatever else the app puts in at issue time. The header names the algorithm, and the signature is the tamper-proof.

items.prompt: Which part of a JWT tells a verifier which algorithm (e.g. HS256) was used to sign it?
choices: The payload
The signature
The header
None — the algorithm is never stored in the token
items.explanation: The header is a small JSON object naming the algorithm (and token type). L3 covers why blindly trusting this field from the token itself, instead of hardcoding the expected algorithm server-side, is a real vulnerability.

items.prompt: A colleague claims a JWT's three parts are interchangeable — you could swap the payload and signature segments and a correct verifier wouldn't notice. Is that true?
choices: True — the three segments are functionally identical blobs of base64
False — the signature is computed specifically over the header+payload bytes in order; swapping segments breaks that byte-for-byte match
True, but only for tokens signed with HS256 specifically
False, but only because the header segment is always exactly the same length
items.explanation: The signature isn't an arbitrary third chunk — it's a value computed from the exact bytes of 'header.payload' in that order. Move the segments around and the verifier recomputes a signature over different bytes than were originally signed, so it won't match.

items.prompt: How many dot-separated parts does a JWT have?
choices: Two
Three
Four
A variable number depending on the algorithm
items.explanation: A JWT is always header.payload.signature — exactly three parts joined by dots.

items.prompt: What is the first part of a JWT called?
choices: Header
Payload
Signature
Footer
items.explanation: The header comes first, and names the signing algorithm and token type.

items.prompt: What encoding are the header and payload segments of a JWT written in?
choices: base64url
Hexadecimal
Plain UTF-8 text with no encoding
Gzip-compressed binary
items.explanation: Header and payload are base64url-encoded JSON — readable with a decoder, not encrypted.

items.prompt: Which claim conventionally identifies which user a JWT's payload is about?
choices: sub
exp
alg
typ
items.explanation: sub (subject) is the conventional claim for 'who this token is about.'

items.prompt: Which claim conventionally holds a token's expiry timestamp?
choices: exp
sub
iat
typ
items.explanation: exp (expiry) is the conventional claim name for when a token should stop being trusted.

items.prompt: What is the signature segment computed over?
choices: The header and payload segments, exactly as sent
Only the payload segment
The user's plaintext password
A random number generated at verify time
items.explanation: The signature is an HMAC (or similar) computed over the header and payload bytes joined by a dot — not over the password or anything else.

items.prompt: Which algorithm name might you see in a JWT header?
choices: HS256
TCP
AES-GCM-TLS
SHA-POST
items.explanation: HS256 (HMAC-SHA256) is a common JWT signing algorithm named in the header.

items.prompt: Can a user open their browser's dev tools, copy their own JWT, and read its payload claims in plain text?
choices: No, the payload is encrypted and requires the secret to read
Yes — the payload is only base64url-encoded, not encrypted
Only if they also happen to know the server's secret key
Only for tokens that have already expired, not active ones
items.explanation: JWTs are signed, not encrypted, by default. Base64url is a reversible encoding, not a cipher — anyone can decode a JWT's header and payload with nothing more than a text editor.

items.prompt: A developer wants to put a user's plaintext password into a JWT payload 'because it's signed, so it's safe.' Is that reasoning sound?
choices: Yes — a signature makes any payload data fully confidential too
No — signing proves integrity, not confidentiality; the payload is still plainly readable
Yes, but only if the token is configured to be short-lived
No — JWTs cannot hold any sensitive data under any circumstances at all
items.explanation: Signing guarantees the payload wasn't tampered with; it does nothing to hide it. Anything placed in a JWT payload should be treated as fully visible to whoever holds the token.

items.prompt: A security review flags that a company's JWTs embed each user's unmasked home address as a convenience for a shipping feature. Why is 'but it's signed' not a sufficient defense here?
choices: It is sufficient — a valid signature means the data can't leak to anyone
Signing only proves the address wasn't altered after the token was issued; anyone who ever holds the token (the browser, an extension, a proxy, a log line) can still read it in plain text
The review is wrong — JWT payloads are always encrypted by every library by default
It's only a problem if the token's exp claim is set too far in the future
items.explanation: The defense conflates two different properties. Signing (integrity) stops silent tampering; it was never designed to stop reading. A signed JWT carrying an address is exactly as exposed to anyone who can see the token as if it were sent in plain, unsigned JSON.

items.prompt: Is a JWT's payload encrypted by default?
choices: No — it's base64url-encoded, which anyone can decode
Yes, always, using the server's secret
Only the exp claim is encrypted
Yes, but only in production environments
items.explanation: By default, a JWT payload is encoded, not encrypted — readable by anyone who has the token.

items.prompt: What does the JWT signature actually protect against?
choices: Tampering with the header or payload after signing
Anyone ever reading the payload
The token being sent over an insecure network
The token being stored in the browser
items.explanation: The signature's job is tamper detection, not confidentiality.

items.prompt: Is base64url the same thing as encryption?
choices: No — it's a reversible encoding, not a cipher
Yes — base64url and encryption are interchangeable terms
Only when combined with HTTPS
Yes, but only for the signature segment
items.explanation: Base64url simply re-represents bytes in a different alphabet; it provides no confidentiality at all.

items.prompt: Should sensitive secrets (like a plaintext password) ever go inside a JWT payload?
choices: No — the payload is readable by anyone holding the token
Yes, as long as the token has an exp claim
Yes, since the payload is always encrypted
Only for tokens signed with RS256
items.explanation: Anything placed in the payload should be treated as visible, not confidential — never put secrets there.

items.prompt: What tool would someone need to read a JWT's claims?
choices: Just a base64url decoder — no secret required
The server's private signing key
A working internet connection to the issuing server
Root access to the server that issued it
items.explanation: Decoding the payload needs nothing more than a base64url decoder, since it's only encoded, not encrypted.

items.prompt: If a JWT needs to carry genuinely confidential data, what's missing from a plain signed JWT?
choices: Encryption of the payload (a separate mechanism from signing)
A longer expiry time
A larger number of claims
A second signature from a different server
items.explanation: Plain JWTs are signed, not encrypted — genuine confidentiality would require an additional encryption step (or simply not putting secrets in the token at all).

items.prompt: Which best describes the relationship between 'readable' and 'tamper-proof' for a standard JWT?
choices: Readable by anyone with the token, but tamper-evident thanks to the signature
Neither readable nor tamper-evident
Tamper-proof but also fully hidden from the holder
Readable only by the server, never by the client
items.explanation: A standard JWT is fully readable to its holder and tamper-evident via the signature — two independent properties, not one.

items.prompt: In a JWT payload, what does the exp claim represent?
choices: The user's self-reported experience level within the application
A timestamp after which the token should no longer be trusted
The number of times this particular token has been used so far
The algorithm's expected output length, in bytes, for this token
items.explanation: exp (expiry) is a Unix timestamp; a verifier should reject the token once the current time passes it.

items.prompt: What does the sub claim conventionally identify in a JWT payload?
choices: The subject line that would appear in a related notification email
The subject — i.e. which user or entity the token is about
The subscription tier currently associated with the account
The server, specifically, that originally issued the token
items.explanation: sub is short for 'subject' — conventionally the user ID (or other principal) the token is asserting facts about.

items.prompt: A token's payload is { "sub": "user_42" } with no exp claim at all. What does that imply about this token's lifetime?
choices: It expires after exactly 24 hours by default, per the JWT spec
There's nothing in the payload itself limiting how long it stays valid — a verifier that only checks the signature would accept it indefinitely
It's automatically invalid, since exp is a mandatory field
It expires as soon as the user's browser tab is closed
items.explanation: exp isn't mandatory at the format level — it's a convention the issuing server chooses to include and the verifier chooses to check. A token missing it has no built-in expiry at all, which is itself a design risk worth flagging, not a format error.

items.prompt: What does 'sub' stand for in a JWT payload?
choices: Subject
Subscription
Submit
Subdomain
items.explanation: sub is short for 'subject' — the entity the token is about.

items.prompt: What does 'exp' stand for in a JWT payload?
choices: Expiry
Experience
Export
Expression
items.explanation: exp is short for 'expiry' — the timestamp after which the token should be rejected.

items.prompt: Who decides what value goes into the sub claim?
choices: The server, at the time it issues the token
The client, when it sends a request
The load balancer, based on routing rules
A separate claims-negotiation protocol
items.explanation: Every claim, including sub, is set by the issuing server — never negotiated afterward.

items.prompt: Besides sub and exp, what else might a JWT payload carry?
choices: App-specific data like role or tenant ID
The user's raw password hash, always
The server's private signing key
The browser's full request history
items.explanation: Beyond the conventional sub/exp claims, a payload can carry whatever app-specific fields the issuing server chooses — roles, tenant IDs, etc.

items.prompt: Is exp a mandatory field in every JWT?
choices: No — it's a convention, not a strict requirement of the format
Yes, every valid JWT must include it
Yes, but only for tokens signed with HS256
No — exp is actually part of the header, not the payload
items.explanation: exp is conventional, widely used, and important to check — but the bare JWT format doesn't force it to be present.

items.prompt: What should a server do once the current time passes a token's exp value?
choices: Reject the token
Automatically refresh it without asking
Ignore exp and keep trusting the token
Re-encrypt the payload
items.explanation: A verifier checking exp should reject the token once the current time is at or past that timestamp.

items.prompt: Is sub typically a human-readable username, or an opaque identifier?
choices: Usually an opaque identifier like a user ID, not necessarily a readable name
Always the user's full legal name
Always the user's email address, by spec
A randomly generated value with no connection to the user
items.explanation: sub is conventionally a stable identifier (often a user ID), not necessarily anything human-readable.

items.prompt: A shared Redis session store lets every server recognize every user, same as a JWT would. Why is the Redis approach still called 'stateful'?
choices: Because Redis happens to be measurably slower than a plain JWT check
Because the session state still lives on a server-side system (Redis) that must stay available
Because Redis is fundamentally incapable of being scaled horizontally
There's no real difference at all — both approaches are equally stateless
items.explanation: Statelessness is about where the session data lives, not about how many servers can access it. A Redis-backed session still depends on a server-side store staying up and reachable; a JWT carries its data in the request itself, with no server-side store at all.

items.prompt: An app uses sticky sessions and an aggressive autoscaler that removes servers every few minutes. Does sticky routing still protect a user's session from being lost?
choices: Yes, sticky sessions fully guarantee the session will always survive
No — once the pinned server is removed, that user's session is gone exactly as before
Yes, as long as the load balancer is configured to retry automatically
No — sticky sessions never actually worked, with or without an autoscaler
items.explanation: Sticky sessions only guarantee routing consistency while the pinned server exists. An autoscaler doesn't coordinate with sticky routing at all — when it removes that server, the in-memory session goes with it.

items.prompt: A team wants 'zero server-side state' but also wants to force-expire a specific user's access within seconds if their account is compromised. Which of the three architectures (sticky, shared store, stateless token) gives them both properties at once, unmodified?
choices: Sticky sessions — pinning solves both requirements
None of them, unmodified — a bare stateless token has no server-side record to revoke instantly, and a shared store isn't 'zero state'; this is the real tension between the two goals
A shared session store, which satisfies 'zero server-side state' by definition
A stateless token, since JWTs can always be revoked instantly by design
items.explanation: This is a trick in the requirements themselves: 'zero server-side state' and 'instant per-user revocation' pull in opposite directions. A bare JWT satisfies the first by giving up the second; a shared store satisfies the second by giving up the first. Getting close to both (L3's denylist/refresh-token approach) means accepting a small, deliberate amount of server-side state back.

items.prompt: Which architecture pins a user to one specific server?
choices: Sticky sessions
Shared session store
Stateless token
None of these
items.explanation: Sticky sessions configure the load balancer to always route a given user back to the same server.

items.prompt: Which architecture is vulnerable to an autoscaler removing the 'pinned' server?
choices: Sticky sessions
Shared session store
Stateless token
All three equally
items.explanation: Only sticky sessions depend on one specific server staying alive — a shared store or stateless token don't care which server handles the request.

items.prompt: Is a shared Redis store 'stateless' or 'stateful'?
choices: Stateful — the session record lives on a server-side system
Stateless — Redis doesn't count as a server
Stateless — any shared system is automatically stateless
Neither term applies to Redis
items.explanation: A shared store is still stateful: the session data lives on a server (Redis) that the whole system depends on staying available.

items.prompt: What's the defining property of a genuinely stateless auth scheme?
choices: No server anywhere has to store session data between requests
Every server shares a database
Requests never time out
Cookies are disabled entirely
items.explanation: Statelessness means no server-side store exists to depend on at all — not just that multiple servers can reach the same store.

items.prompt: Which architecture would keep working seamlessly through aggressive, frequent autoscaling?
choices: A stateless token (JWT)
Sticky sessions
Neither — autoscaling breaks all three equally
Only sticky sessions, if configured correctly
items.explanation: A stateless token has no server-side dependency at all, so adding or removing servers doesn't affect whether a request can be verified.

items.prompt: What's the one thing 'any server can handle any request' does NOT by itself tell you?
choices: Whether a server-side store is depended on behind the scenes
Whether cookies are being used
Whether the token is base64url-encoded
Whether the request used HTTPS
items.explanation: Both a shared store and a stateless token let any server handle any request — that property alone doesn't distinguish stateful from stateless.

items.prompt: What happens to a sticky-session user's login if their pinned server crashes?
choices: The session is lost, same as the original single-server problem
Nothing — sticky sessions replicate data to a backup automatically
The load balancer transparently restores the session elsewhere
The session upgrades automatically into a shared-store session
items.explanation: Sticky sessions don't add any redundancy — if the pinned server goes away, so does whatever it was holding in memory.

items.prompt: When a server verifies a JWT's signature, what is it actually doing?
choices: Looking the token up inside a central, server-side database
Decrypting the token's payload using a stored private key
Recomputing the signature from the received header+payload and comparing it to the one in the token
Checking the token's identifier against a list of banned tokens
items.explanation: Verification recomputes the HMAC (or other algorithm) over the header and payload exactly as received, using the shared secret, and compares the result to the signature already in the token.

items.prompt: Why does JWT verification not require a network call to a database, unlike a shared-session-store lookup?
choices: Because JWTs are, in general, always small enough to cache locally
Because verification is pure computation against a secret the server already holds — nothing external needs to be consulted
Because JWTs are, by design, never actually checked on every request
Because it's the browser, not the server, that performs verification
items.explanation: Signature verification only needs the token itself and the secret/key the verifying server already has locally — there's nothing to look up externally.

items.prompt: Two servers, A and B, both verify JWTs with HS256 but were configured with different signing secrets by mistake. A token issued (and signed) by server A is sent to server B. What happens?
choices: Server B accepts it, since both servers run the same verification code
Server B recomputes the signature with its own (different) secret, gets a different result than the token's actual signature, and rejects the token
Server B automatically fetches server A's secret from the token's header
Server B accepts it only if the payload's sub claim matches a known user
items.explanation: The secret is the actual trust anchor, not the code. Running identical verification logic with a different secret produces a different recomputed signature, which won't match — so the token is rejected exactly as if it had been tampered with. This is why all servers that need to accept each other's tokens must share the same secret (or use asymmetric keys where one signs and many verify).

items.prompt: What does the verifying server recompute during JWT verification?
choices: The signature, from the received header and payload
The user's original password
A new session ID
The token's expiry timestamp from scratch
items.explanation: Verification recomputes the signature over the exact header+payload bytes received, using the known secret.

items.prompt: Does JWT verification require a network call?
choices: No — it's a local computation against a secret the server already has
Yes, always, to the issuing server
Yes, but only for expired tokens
No, but only if the token has no claims at all
items.explanation: Verification is pure local computation — no network round trip needed.

items.prompt: What happens if the recomputed signature doesn't match the one in the token?
choices: The server rejects the token
The server accepts it anyway, with a warning logged
The server asks the client to resend the password
The server retries verification with a different algorithm
items.explanation: A mismatch means the content was altered (or never signed with the right secret) — the correct response is outright rejection.

items.prompt: What does a server need locally to verify a JWT it didn't issue itself?
choices: The same shared secret (or matching public key) used to sign it
A live connection to the original issuing server
The user's original login password
Nothing — any server can verify any token with no shared setup
items.explanation: Verification requires knowing the signing secret (symmetric) or a matching public key (asymmetric) — some shared trust setup is unavoidable.

items.prompt: Is JWT verification free, in terms of cost?
choices: No — it costs CPU time, just not a network round trip
Yes, completely free, with zero cost of any kind
No — it costs more than a database lookup, always
Yes, but only for tokens under 100 bytes
items.explanation: Verification isn't literally free — it costs CPU time for the cryptographic computation — it just avoids the network cost a shared-store lookup would add.

items.prompt: Why does signature verification scale to any number of servers with no added infrastructure?
choices: Because each server verifies independently, with no coordination needed beyond already knowing the secret
Because JWTs are cached globally by every CDN automatically
Because only one designated server is ever allowed to verify tokens
Because verification doesn't actually check anything meaningful
items.explanation: Each server can verify on its own, in isolation, as long as it already has the shared secret — no central coordination point is needed per request.

items.prompt: What's the first thing a verifying server needs before it can recompute a signature?
choices: The header and payload bytes exactly as received
The user's current IP address
A fresh session ID issued moments earlier
The browser's user-agent string
items.explanation: Verification recomputes the signature from the received header+payload bytes — that's the input the whole check is built on.

items.prompt: Who decides what values go into a JWT's claims (like role or tenantId)?
choices: The client, at the moment it sends the request to the server
The issuing server, at the moment it signs the token
Whoever currently holds the token, at any point afterward
The load balancer, based on whatever its routing rules say
items.explanation: Claims are set by the server at issue time (login), then locked in by the signature. The client can read them afterward but has no legitimate way to change them.

items.prompt: A client sends a request with a JWT whose payload has been decoded, edited to add "role":"admin", and re-encoded — without re-signing. What happens on verification?
choices: The server accepts it, since role is treated as ordinary data
The server rejects it — the recomputed signature won't match the edited payload
The server silently ignores the edited role claim and moves on
The server automatically upgrades the user's role to match it
items.explanation: Any edit to the payload changes the bytes fed into signature recomputation. Without the secret to produce a matching signature for the new payload, verification fails.

items.prompt: A frontend developer argues: 'since the client can already read every claim in its own JWT, it should be fine for the client to also send its own updated claims object alongside the token, and have the server just trust the fresher one.' What's wrong with that proposal?
choices: Nothing — reading and writing claims are equally safe once a token has been issued

It throws away the entire trust model: anyone could then set role, tenantId, or any other claim to whatever they want, since the server would be trusting client-supplied data instead of the signed token
It's fine as long as the request is sent over HTTPS
It's only a problem if the user account in question happens to be an admin
items.explanation: Being readable and being trustworthy are different properties. The whole reason claims are safe to act on is that they're locked by a signature only the server could produce. A 'trust whatever the client also sends' fallback reintroduces exactly the vulnerability signing exists to prevent — client-controlled authorization data.

items.prompt: Who sets the value of the role claim in a JWT?
choices: The issuing server, at login time
The client, whenever it wants
The load balancer
Whichever server verifies the token last
items.explanation: All claims are set by the server at issue time — never by the client afterward.

items.prompt: Can the client read the claims inside its own JWT?
choices: Yes — reading is always possible since the payload is just encoded
No, claims are fully hidden from the client
Only the sub claim is readable, never others
Only if the token has already expired
items.explanation: The client can always read its own token's claims, since they're only base64url-encoded.

items.prompt: Can the client change a claim's value and have the server still trust it?
choices: No — any edit breaks the signature match on verification
Yes, as long as the edit is small
Yes, for claims other than sub and exp
Yes, if the client re-encodes it correctly
items.explanation: Editing the payload changes the bytes the signature was computed over — the server's recomputed signature won't match, so the edit is detected.

items.prompt: What's the difference between 'the client can read this' and 'the client can influence this,' for a JWT's claims?
choices: Reading is always true; influencing is false as long as signatures are verified
They're the same thing for JWTs
Influencing is always true; reading is false
Neither is ever true for a properly configured JWT
items.explanation: A client can always read a claim (it's just encoded) but can't legitimately influence it, because any change invalidates the signature.

items.prompt: At what point are a JWT's claims locked in?
choices: At signing time, when the server issues the token
Only once the token expires
Only after the first successful verification
Never — they can always be updated in place
items.explanation: Claims are fixed the moment the token is signed — the signature is what makes later tampering detectable.

items.prompt: If a server always verifies the signature before trusting any claim, what's the practical result?
choices: Only values the server itself originally set can ever be trusted as claims
The client can set any claim it wants safely
Claims become irrelevant to authorization decisions
The signature step can be skipped for read-only requests
items.explanation: Because verification catches any tampering, trusting a claim post-verification is equivalent to trusting whatever the issuing server originally wrote.

items.prompt: Why is role a risky claim to leave unchecked by signature verification?
choices: Because an attacker could set it to something privileged, like 'admin', if verification is skipped
Because role is always encrypted separately from other claims
Because role claims expire faster than other claims
Because role is not technically allowed in the JWT spec
items.explanation: role (or any authorization-relevant claim) is exactly the kind of value an attacker would want to forge — which is why signature verification before trusting any claim is non-negotiable.

items.prompt: A support engineer needs to immediately force-logout a compromised account. Which is easier to do instantly: a shared-store session, or a bare JWT?
choices: A bare JWT — the holder can simply discard it whenever they like
A shared-store session — delete the record and the very next lookup fails
Both are equally instant to revoke, with no meaningful difference
Neither one can ever be revoked once it's been issued to a client
items.explanation: A shared session store can delete the record immediately, so the next lookup fails right away. A bare JWT has no server-side record at all — it stays valid to any verifying server until its own exp claim passes.

items.prompt: What does verifying a JWT cost per request, compared to a shared-store lookup?
choices: Exactly the same — both need a network call
A local signature computation (CPU), with no network round trip
Nothing at all — verification is free
More than a shared-store lookup, since crypto is always slower than a query
items.explanation: JWT verification is a local cryptographic computation — no network call required. It's not literally free, but it avoids the network round trip a shared-store lookup requires on every request.

items.prompt: A team switches from a shared Redis session store to bare JWTs to cut their per-request latency, but keeps no fallback plan for compromised-account logout. Six months later, a support engineer needs to force-logout a user whose laptop was stolen. What's their actual option with a bare JWT, right now?
choices: Delete the user's session record — it will take effect on the very next request
Nothing immediate — without a denylist or short-lived-token/refresh-token scheme already in place, the token stays valid to any server until its own exp passes
Ask the issuing server to re-sign a new token with the same secret, invalidating the old one automatically
Instruct the CDN to drop all requests from that user's IP address
items.explanation: This is the cost of the earlier latency win showing up later: a bare JWT genuinely has nothing to revoke. Without the mitigations L3 covers (short expiry + refresh tokens, or a denylist) built in from the start, the only real lever left is waiting for exp — which is exactly the gap those mitigations exist to close.

items.prompt: Can a bare JWT be revoked the instant it's issued, with no other mechanism in place?
choices: No — there's no server-side record to delete
Yes, by asking the browser to discard it
Yes, automatically, once any claim changes
No, but only for tokens signed with RS256
items.explanation: A bare JWT has nothing stored server-side to delete — 'revoke it' has no target until it expires on its own.

items.prompt: What makes a shared-store session easy to revoke instantly?
choices: The server-side record can simply be deleted
It's always encrypted with a rotating key
It never has an exp claim to check
It's stored in the URL, not a cookie
items.explanation: A shared store's session record can be deleted directly — the very next lookup against it fails immediately.

items.prompt: Does JWT verification require a network round trip?
choices: No — it's a local CPU computation
Yes, to the database every time
Yes, but only on the first request
No, but only if the token has fewer than 5 claims
items.explanation: Verification is local; nothing about it requires reaching out over a network.

items.prompt: Does a shared-store lookup require a network round trip?
choices: Yes — it's a real network cost on every request
No, it's always resolved locally
Only on the very first request per session
Only if the store happens to be remote, which is rare
items.explanation: A shared store is, by definition, a separate system most servers reach over the network — that's a genuine per-request cost.

items.prompt: What's the main trade-off between bare JWTs and shared-store sessions?
choices: Cheap, no-lookup verification vs. the ability to revoke instantly
Encryption strength vs. token size
Browser compatibility vs. server compatibility
Cookie support vs. header support
items.explanation: The core trade-off: JWTs are cheap to verify but hard to revoke; shared-store sessions cost a lookup but revoke instantly.

items.prompt: Until what point does a bare JWT, with no other mitigation, stay valid once issued?
choices: Until its own exp claim passes
Until the user closes their browser
Until the next server restart
Forever, with no limit of any kind
items.explanation: Without a denylist or refresh-token scheme, a bare JWT's only built-in limit is its exp claim.

items.prompt: Is 'cheap per-request verification' and 'instant revocation' something a bare JWT gets both of at once?
choices: No — it gets cheap verification at the cost of instant revocation
Yes, both, with no trade-off at all
No — it gets neither property
Yes, but only for tokens under a certain size
items.explanation: This is the central trade-off of stateless auth: the same thing that makes verification cheap (no server-side record) is what makes instant revocation impossible without an added mechanism.

items.prompt: Standard base64 output can contain +, /, and trailing = characters. Why does base64url replace or strip these before a value is embedded in a JWT?
choices: Because base64url is faster to compute than standard base64
Because +, /, and = are meaningful in URLs (and awkward in a dot-separated token), so they'd clash with where the encoded value is actually used
Because standard base64 cannot represent all byte values
Because JSON doesn't allow the characters +, /, or =
items.explanation: + can be read as a space in a URL, / looks like a path separator, and = is often a query-parameter delimiter or padding marker — all problematic inside a value meant to sit directly in a URL or a dot-separated token. base64url substitutes - for + and _ for /, and drops the padding entirely, specifically to avoid those clashes.

items.prompt: A JWT library correctly base64url-encodes the header and payload, but a teammate's code manually concatenates them with a comma instead of a dot ("header,payload,signature") before sending. What breaks?
choices: Nothing — any separator character works as long as it's consistent

Any standard-compliant verifier splitting on "." won't find the expected 3 parts, and the signature (which was computed over header.payload with a dot) won't match what a correct verifier reconstructs
The token becomes more secure, since commas aren't valid in URLs
The payload will fail to decode as JSON regardless of the separator used
items.explanation: The dot isn't cosmetic — it's part of the exact byte sequence ('header.payload') that gets signed, and part of what every standard verifier splits on. Changing the separator breaks interoperability with any correctly implemented verifier, even though each individual segment is still validly encoded on its own.

items.prompt: Why must a correct base64url decoder restore padding (=) before calling atob(), even though a correct encoder deliberately strips it?
choices: atob() only accepts input whose length is a multiple of 4, and padding is what the standard base64 alphabet uses to reach that multiple — stripping it for transport doesn't remove the underlying length requirement
Padding is needed to add extra randomness to the decoded bytes
atob() automatically re-adds any missing padding on its own, so this step is actually unnecessary
Padding encodes the original string's character encoding (UTF-8 vs UTF-16)
items.explanation: base64's 4-characters-per-3-bytes scheme needs the input length to be a multiple of 4; padding exists purely to pad a final short group up to that boundary. base64url removes it because it's unnecessary clutter in a URL/token context, but the browser's atob() still expects standard base64 input — so a correct decoder has to compute and re-add exactly the missing amount before decoding.

items.prompt: What does base64url replace the standard base64 '+' character with?
items.explanation: base64url substitutes - for the standard base64 '+' character.

items.prompt: What does base64url replace the standard base64 '/' character with?
items.explanation: base64url substitutes _ for the standard base64 '/' character.

items.prompt: Does base64url output include trailing = padding?
choices: No — it's stripped
Yes, always
Only for odd-length inputs
Only in the signature segment
items.explanation: base64url deliberately drops the trailing = padding that standard base64 includes.

items.prompt: Why would '+' be a problem if left unescaped inside a URL?
choices: It can be interpreted as a space character
It's not a valid ASCII character
It makes the string longer than necessary
It conflicts with JSON's object syntax
items.explanation: In URL encoding contexts, '+' is often interpreted as a space — exactly the kind of ambiguity base64url avoids by substituting a different character.

items.prompt: What character joins the three parts of a JWT together?
items.explanation: A JWT's three segments — header, payload, signature — are joined by dots.

items.prompt: Does browser atob() accept base64url input directly, without any adjustment?
choices: No — padding and character substitutions need to be reversed first
Yes, atob() handles base64url natively
Yes, but only for strings under 100 characters
No — atob() only works on already-decoded text
items.explanation: atob() expects standard base64, so a correct decoder must undo base64url's substitutions and restore padding first.

items.prompt: What's the relationship between a string's raw byte count and its base64-encoded size?
choices: The encoded size is roughly 4/3 of the raw byte count
The encoded size is always exactly equal to the raw byte count
The encoded size is always half the raw byte count
There's no predictable relationship between the two
items.explanation: Base64 represents every 3 raw bytes as 4 encoded characters, so encoded output runs about 4/3 the size of the original bytes.

items.prompt: A token arrives as the string "aa.bb" — only two parts. What should a well-written verify function do with it?
choices: Treat it as a token missing only its signature, and check the payload anyway
Reject it immediately as structurally malformed, before attempting any decoding
Assume the signature is empty and treat the token as unsigned but valid
Pad it with an empty third segment and continue as normal
items.explanation: A JWT is always exactly 3 dot-separated, non-empty segments. Anything else — too few, too many, or an empty segment — is structurally invalid and should be rejected outright, before any base64url decoding or JSON parsing is attempted on data that might not even be well-formed enough to decode.

items.prompt: Why is throwing an error better than returning undefined from a function that extracts a token's signature segment, when the token turns out to be malformed?
choices: Throwing forces every caller to handle the invalid case explicitly, instead of risking a confusing comparison against undefined several steps later
Throwing is required by the JWT specification itself
Returning undefined would cause a syntax error at the call site
There's no real difference — both approaches are equally safe in practice
items.explanation: A silent undefined can slip through later logic (e.g. compared against another value, producing a confusing false result) without anyone noticing the real problem was a malformed token several steps earlier. An explicit throw stops the problem at its source and forces it to be handled.

items.prompt: A developer writes a structural check using token.split(".", 3) — passing a limit argument to split — believing it correctly rejects tokens with extra segments. Does it?
choices: Yes — split with a limit always rejects anything beyond that count

No — split(separator, limit) stops collecting once it reaches the limit and silently discards everything after, so a 4-part token like "aa.bb.cc.dd" still produces exactly 3 parts and passes the check
No, but only for tokens longer than 1000 characters
Yes, as long as every segment is non-empty
items.explanation: JavaScript's split(separator, limit) caps how many results it returns — it does not verify there was nothing left over. A genuinely 4-part token truncates down to the same 3-element array a correct 3-part token would produce, so the extra segment goes completely undetected. Splitting with no limit and checking the full resulting array length is the only way to actually catch it.

items.prompt: How many non-empty segments must a well-formed JWT have?
choices: Exactly 3
At least 2
Exactly 4
Any number, as long as it's odd
items.explanation: A well-formed JWT always has exactly 3 non-empty, dot-separated segments.

items.prompt: Is "aa..cc" (an empty middle segment) a well-formed JWT?
choices: No — one of its segments is empty
Yes — 3 segments is 3 segments
Yes, but only if the empty segment is the signature
No, because it has too many dots
items.explanation: Even though it splits into 3 parts, one of them is empty — a well-formed JWT requires all 3 segments to be non-empty.

items.prompt: Should structural validation (checking part count) happen before or after decoding the payload?
choices: Before — reject malformed shapes before attempting to decode anything
After — decode first, then check the shape
It doesn't matter which order they happen in
Only after signature verification has already passed
items.explanation: Checking the basic shape first avoids attempting to decode or parse data that might not even be structurally valid JWT data.

items.prompt: What's a safer alternative to returning undefined when a structural check fails?
choices: Throwing an explicit error
Returning the string "invalid"
Returning 0
Logging a warning and continuing silently
items.explanation: Throwing forces the caller to explicitly handle the malformed case, rather than letting a silent undefined propagate into later logic.

items.prompt: Does String.prototype.split(separator, limit) detect extra segments beyond the limit?
choices: No — it silently discards anything past the limit
Yes — it throws if there are more segments than the limit
Yes — it returns an array longer than the limit to signal the overflow
No — it always returns exactly 2 segments regardless of input
items.explanation: split with a limit argument just stops collecting once it reaches that count — it never checks or reports whether more segments existed.

items.prompt: What does a 4-part token like "aa.bb.cc.dd" indicate?
choices: A structurally invalid JWT — it has one segment too many
A JWT using an extended 4-segment format
A JWT with two signatures for extra security
A perfectly normal JWT with an optional metadata segment
items.explanation: The JWT format is always exactly 3 segments — a 4th segment makes the token structurally invalid, not an extension of the format.

items.prompt: Why check structure before trusting any of a token's claims?
choices: Because a malformed token shouldn't reach claims-reading logic at all
Because structure checks are faster than signature checks, so order doesn't matter otherwise
Because claims can only be read after structure is confirmed valid JSON
There's no real reason — order doesn't matter
items.explanation: A structurally malformed token should be rejected outright, before any attempt to decode or reason about claims it might contain.

items.prompt: A JWT's exp claim is a Unix timestamp in seconds. A verify function compares it directly against JavaScript's Date.now(). What goes wrong?
choices: Nothing — Date.now() and exp use the same units by default
Date.now() returns milliseconds, roughly 1000x larger than exp's seconds, so an unexpired token can look expired immediately
The comparison throws a type error, since one is a number and one is a string
exp claims are always invalid after this comparison, regardless of the actual expiry time
items.explanation: exp is defined in Unix seconds; Date.now() returns milliseconds since epoch. Comparing them directly without converting makes 'now' appear roughly 1000 times further in the future than it actually is, relative to exp — so almost any real token (with exp some reasonable time in the future, in seconds) ends up looking already expired.

items.prompt: An expiry check uses strict greater-than (now > exp) instead of greater-than-or-equal (now >= exp) to decide if a token is expired. What's the practical effect, at the exact expiry second?
choices: None — the two comparisons are always equivalent
A token is treated as still valid for one extra second, exactly at its exp timestamp, instead of already expired
The token becomes permanently invalid one second early instead of late
It causes the signature check to fail unexpectedly
items.explanation: At now == exp, now > exp is false (not yet expired) while now >= exp is true (expired). It's a one-second edge case, but it's the kind of off-by-one that matters for a security boundary — most real JWT libraries treat the exact expiry second as already expired, which is what >= captures.

items.prompt: A payload has no exp claim at all, and a verify function's expiry check is written as 'if now >= payload.exp, reject.' What happens when payload.exp is undefined?
choices: The comparison now >= undefined evaluates to false, so the check never rejects — but this accidentally relies on a quirk of comparing to undefined rather than an explicit 'no exp means never expires' rule
The function throws a TypeError immediately
undefined is treated as 0, so the token is always rejected as already expired
undefined is treated as Infinity, making the token correctly never expire, by design
items.explanation: Comparing any number to undefined (now >= undefined) evaluates to false in JavaScript, which happens to produce the 'right' outcome here — but only by accident. A correct implementation should check typeof payload.exp === 'number' explicitly and treat a missing exp as 'never expires' on purpose, not rely on an easily-forgotten quirk of how undefined compares.

items.prompt: What unit is a JWT's exp claim conventionally expressed in?
choices: Unix seconds
Milliseconds since epoch
Minutes since midnight
ISO 8601 date strings
items.explanation: exp is conventionally a Unix timestamp in seconds, not milliseconds.

items.prompt: What unit does JavaScript's Date.now() return?
choices: Milliseconds since epoch
Seconds since epoch
Minutes since epoch
Microseconds since epoch
items.explanation: Date.now() returns the number of milliseconds since the Unix epoch.

items.prompt: What has to happen before comparing Date.now() directly to an exp claim?
choices: Divide Date.now() by 1000 to convert it to seconds
Multiply exp by 1000 to convert it to milliseconds and leave Date.now() as is — either works, as long as they're consistent
Nothing — they're already in the same unit
Round exp to the nearest minute first
items.explanation: Since exp is in seconds and Date.now() is in milliseconds, one of the two values needs converting before the comparison is meaningful (dividing Date.now() by 1000 is the common approach).

items.prompt: At the exact moment now equals exp, should the token be considered expired?
choices: Yes — treating the exact expiry second as already expired is the common convention
No — it should remain valid for one more full second
It depends on which programming language is used
exp is never checked for exact equality, only inequality
items.explanation: Most implementations treat now >= exp (inclusive) as expired, so the exact expiry instant itself counts as expired.

items.prompt: Should a payload with no exp claim at all be treated as expired?
choices: No — a missing exp means there's no expiry to check against
Yes, immediately, as a safety default
Only if the token is older than 24 hours
Yes, unless the sub claim is present
items.explanation: No exp claim means there's nothing to compare against — such a token should be treated as never expiring by this check (though omitting exp entirely is itself a design concern worth flagging).

items.prompt: Why is a strict mismatch between seconds and milliseconds dangerous here, specifically?
choices: It can make a perfectly valid token appear already expired, or a long-expired token appear still valid
It only affects how the expiry date is displayed in logs, not actual behavior
It causes a crash rather than a silent logic error
It only matters for tokens issued more than a year ago
items.explanation: Because the factor is roughly 1000x, a units mix-up pushes the comparison far enough off that it silently produces the wrong accept/reject decision, not just a cosmetic display issue.

items.prompt: What's a safer way to treat a missing exp claim than relying on how it compares to undefined?
choices: Explicitly check typeof payload.exp === 'number' before comparing
Assume it's always present and skip the check
Treat any missing claim as an immediate rejection
Convert undefined to the string 'expired'
items.explanation: An explicit type check makes the 'no exp means never expires' behavior intentional and readable, instead of depending on an easy-to-forget quirk of comparing numbers to undefined.

items.prompt: Why does adding a single short claim to a JWT payload increase the token's size by more than that claim's raw character count?
choices: Because every claim is encrypted individually before being added
Because base64 encoding expands raw bytes by roughly 4/3, so the JSON structure's extra bytes (quotes, braces, the field name itself) all get inflated on top of the claim's own content
Because adding any claim resets the token's signature to a longer format
It doesn't — base64 encoding has no effect on payload size
items.explanation: The raw bytes added include not just the claim's value but its JSON key, quotes, and punctuation — all of which then get expanded by base64's roughly 4/3 ratio when the payload is re-encoded. The visible size increase is always somewhat larger than the claim's 'useful' content alone.

items.prompt: A team is deciding between adding five individual boolean role flags (canEdit, canDelete, canInvite, canExport, canBill) versus one array of permission strings to a JWT payload. From a pure byte-budget perspective, which consideration matters most?
choices: Arrays are always smaller than separate boolean fields, regardless of content
Both approaches add real bytes per entry — the actual budget question is how many such entries are needed and how often the token is sent, not which JSON shape is used
Boolean flags take up zero bytes since true/false are primitives
Only the first claim added to a payload counts toward the size budget
items.explanation: Neither JSON shape is free — both an array of permission strings and five separate boolean flags add real bytes that get base64-expanded like everything else. The meaningful question for a size budget is the total number of claim-equivalents being carried and how often the token travels (every request, for however many users), not a micro-optimization between two roughly similar JSON encodings.

items.prompt: A mobile app sends its JWT on every API call, including on a cellular connection in low-signal areas. The team considers embedding a user's full permission list (20+ entries) directly in the token to avoid an extra lookup. What's the real trade-off being made?
choices: There's no trade-off — bigger tokens have no practical downside
Saving one server-side lookup per session, at the cost of a bigger payload sent on every single request, including on constrained connections where that recurring cost is felt the most
The token becomes impossible to verify once it exceeds a certain size
This only affects token issuance, not the ongoing cost of every subsequent request
items.explanation: This is exactly the recurring-cost trade-off: stuffing more into the token avoids a one-time lookup cost but adds bytes to every single request from then on. On a constrained connection, that recurring per-request cost is far more noticeable than the lookup it was meant to avoid — the opposite of where the convenience actually pays off.

items.prompt: Does adding a claim to a JWT payload increase the token's overall size?
choices: Yes — every claim adds bytes to the final encoded token
No — claims are free once the header exists
Only if the claim's value is a string, not a number
No — only the signature segment has a fixed size
items.explanation: Every claim added contributes bytes to the payload, which then get base64-encoded into the final token.

items.prompt: Roughly how much does base64 encoding expand raw byte count?
choices: About 4/3 the original size
Exactly double the original size
It shrinks the size by about 25%
It has no effect on size at all
items.explanation: Base64 represents every 3 raw bytes as 4 characters, so encoded output is about 4/3 the size of the raw bytes.

items.prompt: Is a bigger JWT more expensive to send on every request, or only at login?
choices: On every request it's included in, not just at login
Only once, at the moment of login
Only when the token is being verified, not sent
Never — token size has no bandwidth cost
items.explanation: A larger token means more bytes sent with every single request that carries it, not a one-time cost.

items.prompt: Does a claim's JSON key name (e.g. "canEdit") also count toward the token's size?
choices: Yes — the key name, quotes, and punctuation all add bytes too
No — only the value counts, never the key
No — JSON keys are stripped before encoding
Only for keys longer than 10 characters
items.explanation: The entire JSON structure — keys, quotes, braces, commas — contributes bytes, not just the bare values.

items.prompt: What's one reason to avoid stuffing a user's entire profile into a JWT's claims, purely for convenience?
choices: It makes every request that carries the token bigger, permanently, not just the one place the data was convenient to grab
JWT payloads have a hard-coded maximum of 5 claims
Profile data cannot legally be stored in a JWT under any circumstances
It would make the signature invalid
items.explanation: The convenience of having data 'right there' in the token comes at a recurring cost: every future request pays the byte cost of carrying it, whether or not that specific request needed it.

items.prompt: On a slow or constrained network connection, why does token size matter more than it might on a fast connection?
choices: Every extra byte sent repeatedly is proportionally more costly when bandwidth or latency is already tight
Slow connections silently truncate large tokens
Token size has no relationship to network speed
Constrained connections reject any token over a fixed size automatically
items.explanation: The recurring per-request byte cost of a larger token is felt most where bandwidth is already scarce — the same absolute byte increase matters more on a weak connection.

items.prompt: Is there a one-time or a recurring cost to adding claims to a JWT payload?
choices: A recurring cost — paid on every request the token is sent with
A one-time cost, paid only at issuance
No cost at all, in either sense
A recurring cost, but only for the signature segment
items.explanation: Because the token travels with every request, any size increase from added claims is paid again and again, not just once.

items.prompt: A middleware function splits a token, base64url-decodes the payload, and returns it for use in an authorization decision — without calling any signature-checking function anywhere in the code. What's the exploit this enables?
choices: None — decoding the payload is itself sufficient proof of authenticity
An attacker can construct their own header.payload.anything, setting any claim (like role: 'admin') to whatever they want, since nothing ever checks whether it was legitimately signed
The exploit only works if the attacker also knows the server's secret key
This only matters for tokens that have already expired
items.explanation: Decoding just reads bytes — it proves nothing about who produced them. Without a signature check, an attacker doesn't need to steal a valid token or know any secret; they can simply fabricate a payload with whatever claims they want and the function will return it as if it were legitimate.

items.prompt: A JWT library historically trusted the alg field inside a token's own header to decide which algorithm to verify with. An attacker sets "alg": "none" and strips the signature entirely. What makes this dangerous, specifically?
choices: Nothing — a library always falls back to a safe default algorithm when alg is 'none'
If the library honors the token's own claimed algorithm, it skips cryptographic verification altogether for a token that claims to need none — accepting an entirely unsigned forgery
This attack only works against tokens signed with RS256, never HS256
'alg: none' causes every library to throw an error immediately, by specification
items.explanation: The structural fix is never letting the token pick its own verification method — hardcoding the expected algorithm (e.g. always verify as HMAC-SHA256) server-side closes this off entirely, regardless of what the token's header claims about itself.

items.prompt: A reviewer says a decodeClaimsUnsafe(token) helper — one that decodes and returns a payload with no signature check — is inherently a security bug and should be deleted. Is that the right call?
choices: Yes, always — any function that decodes a JWT without verifying it should never exist in a codebase

Not necessarily — decoding without verifying is fine for things like logging or debugging display, as long as the result is never used for an authorization decision; the bug is trusting unverified data, not decoding it
No — decoding and verifying are the same operation, so the distinction doesn't matter
Yes, because decoding a payload always requires the signing secret anyway
items.explanation: Decoding and trusting are genuinely separate operations. A function that only decodes (clearly named to say so) is harmless on its own — logging a token's claims for debugging doesn't need a signature check. The actual bug in the opening scenario's PR was using an unverified decode result to make an authorization decision, not the existence of a decode-only helper.

items.prompt: Does decoding a JWT's payload prove the token is legitimate?
choices: No — decoding just reads bytes; it proves nothing about who produced them
Yes — a payload that decodes cleanly as JSON must be legitimate
Yes, as long as the payload contains a sub claim
No, but only for tokens longer than 100 characters
items.explanation: Decoding is purely mechanical — any string with the right base64url/JSON shape decodes, legitimate or forged.

items.prompt: Can an attacker construct a fake JWT payload without knowing the server's signing secret?
choices: Yes — anyone can build header.payload.anything; the secret is only needed to produce a signature that will actually verify
No — constructing any payload at all requires the secret
Yes, but only for tokens with no exp claim
No — payload construction requires access to the server's codebase
items.explanation: Building the payload itself needs no secret at all — the secret only matters for producing a signature that a real verifier will accept.

items.prompt: What does the alg: none attack rely on?
choices: A verifier trusting the algorithm named inside the token's own header instead of hardcoding it
A flaw in the base64url encoding scheme itself
The attacker already knowing the signing secret
A bug in how JSON.parse handles empty strings
items.explanation: The vulnerability only exists if the verifier lets the token's own header dictate which algorithm (or none) to check against.

items.prompt: What's the structural fix for the alg: none vulnerability?
choices: Hardcode the expected algorithm server-side; never let the token choose
Make the alg field longer so it can't be set to 'none'
Encrypt the header in addition to the payload
Reject any token with a header shorter than 20 bytes
items.explanation: The fix isn't a patch against one specific value — it's never trusting the token's own claim about which algorithm to use.

items.prompt: Is decoding a JWT's payload for debugging/logging purposes inherently unsafe?
choices: No — decoding alone is harmless; the danger is using unverified data for an authorization decision
Yes — any decode operation is a security risk
Yes, but only if the log output is publicly accessible
No, but only if the token has already expired
items.explanation: The operation that's dangerous is trusting unverified claims for something like authorization — plain decoding for display or logging is a separate, harmless action.

items.prompt: What should a verify function check before trusting any decoded claim?
choices: That the signature is valid
That the payload is shorter than 500 bytes
That the sub claim is alphabetically sorted
Nothing — decoding successfully is sufficient
items.explanation: Signature validity is the one check that actually establishes whether decoded claims came from a legitimate issuer.

items.prompt: In the opening PR-review scenario, what single missing step turned a working-looking function into a serious vulnerability?
choices: No call to any signature-checking function anywhere in the code
Using atob() instead of a dedicated base64url library
Not checking the exp claim
Not logging the decoded payload for auditing
items.explanation: The function decoded and returned claims with nothing ever verifying the signature — exactly the gap that lets a forged token sail through unchecked.
